mods.title: JavaScript Foundations & Syntax
mods.excerpt: Start your journey right. Learn how JS runs in the browser, declare variables with let/const, understand data types, operators, and write your first real programs.
mods.body:
JavaScript is the language of the web. It runs in every browser, on servers (via Node.js), and even on IoT devices. Unlike HTML and CSS, JavaScript is a programming language — it can think, calculate, and make decisions.

How JavaScript Runs

When you load a web page, the browser reads your HTML, finds <script> tags, and executes the JavaScript inside them. JS is interpreted (compiled Just-In-Time in modern engines) and single-threaded — it does one thing at a time, but does it very fast.

// Inline script (not recommended for production)
<script>
  console.log("Hello, World!");
</script>

// External script (best practice)
<script src="app.js"></script>

Variables: let, const, and the forbidden var

Variables are containers for storing data. In modern JavaScript, you have two choices:

  • const — Use this by default. The value cannot be reassigned. But objects/arrays declared with const can still be mutated!
  • let — Use when the value will change (counters, accumulators, loop variables).
const username = "sarah_dev";      // Cannot reassign
let score = 0;                     // Will change
score = 100;                       // ✅ Allowed
// username = "john";              // ❌ TypeError!

const user = { name: "Sarah" };
user.name = "John";                // ✅ Allowed! Object mutated, not reassigned.
Golden Rule: Default to const. Switch to let only when the compiler complains. Never use var — it has function scope (not block scope) and allows hoisting bugs.

Primitive Data Types

JavaScript has 7 primitive types. A primitive is a simple, immutable value.

const name   = "Alice";     // string
const age    = 25;          // number (JS has no int/float separation)
const isDev  = true;        // boolean
const empty  = null;        // null — intentional absence of value
const notSet = undefined;   // undefined — variable declared but not assigned
const bigNum = 9007199254740991n; // bigint — for huge integers
const sym    = Symbol("id");      // symbol — unique identifier

Type Coercion: The Silent Bug Maker

JavaScript is loosely typed. It will automatically convert types when operators expect different ones. This is the #1 source of bugs for beginners.

console.log("5" + 3);   // "53"  (string concatenation)
console.log("5" - 3);   // 2     (string coerced to number)
console.log("5" == 5);  // true  (loose equality — coerces!)
console.log("5" === 5); // false (strict equality — NO coercion)

// Always use === and !==
// == performs type coercion before comparison — unpredictable!

Template Literals

Backticks (`) allow multi-line strings and string interpolation with ${}.

const name = "Maya";
const role = "Frontend Dev";

// Old way (concatenation)
const oldBio = "Name: " + name + ", Role: " + role;

// Modern way (template literal)
const bio = `Name: ${name}, Role: ${role}`;

// Multi-line without \n
const html = `
  <div class="card">
    <h2>${name}</h2>
    <p>${role}</p>
  </div>
`;

mods.title: Control Flow & Logic
mods.excerpt: Programs need to make decisions. Master if/else, switch statements, ternary operators, and all loop types to control exactly what your code does and when.
mods.body:
Control flow determines the order in which statements are executed. Without it, your program would just run top-to-bottom like a recipe. With it, your program can react, adapt, and repeat.

if / else if / else

The most common decision structure. JavaScript evaluates conditions and executes the first block that is truthy.

const age = 19;

if (age < 13) {
  console.log("Child");
} else if (age < 20) {
  console.log("Teenager");  // ✅ This runs
} else {
  console.log("Adult");
}

Truthy & Falsy Values

In a boolean context (like an if condition), every value is either "truthy" or "falsy". These 6 values are falsy:

if (false)      // falsy
if (0)          // falsy
if ("")         // falsy (empty string)
if (null)       // falsy
if (undefined)  // falsy
if (NaN)        // falsy (Not a Number)

// Everything else is truthy — including "0", "false", [], and {}
if ("0")        // truthy! Non-empty string
if ([])         // truthy! Empty array is still an object

The Ternary Operator

A compact if/else for simple assignments. Use it for clean, readable code — but don't nest ternaries!

const isLoggedIn = true;

// Instead of:
let message;
if (isLoggedIn) {
  message = "Welcome back!";
} else {
  message = "Please log in.";
}

// Use:
const message = isLoggedIn ? "Welcome back!" : "Please log in.";

// Multiple conditions (use sparingly)
const status = age < 13 ? "child" : age < 20 ? "teen" : "adult";

switch Statements

Use switch when you have many conditions based on the same variable. Always include break to prevent fall-through.

const role = "admin";

switch (role) {
  case "admin":
    console.log("Full access granted");
    break;  // Exit the switch
  case "editor":
    console.log("Can edit content");
    break;
  case "viewer":
    console.log("Read-only access");
    break;
  default:
    console.log("Unknown role");
}

Loops

Loops repeat code. Choose the right one for the job:

// for loop — when you know how many iterations
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
}

// while loop — when condition is checked BEFORE each iteration
let countdown = 3;
while (countdown > 0) {
  console.log(countdown);
  countdown--;
}

// do...while — runs at least ONCE, then checks condition
let input;
do {
  input = prompt("Enter a number greater than 10:");
} while (input <= 10);

// for...of — iterate over ITERABLES (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets)
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
for (const fruit of fruits) {
  console.log(fruit);
}

// for...in — iterate over KEYS of an object (avoid for arrays!)
const person = { name: "Alex", age: 30 };
for (const key in person) {
  console.log(key, person[key]); // "name" "Alex", "age" 30
}

break & continue

// break — exit the loop entirely
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  if (i === 5) break;
  console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
}

// continue — skip to next iteration
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  if (i === 2) continue;
  console.log(i); // 0, 1, 3, 4
}

mods.title: Functions Deep Dive
mods.excerpt: Functions are the building blocks of JavaScript. Learn declarations vs expressions, arrow functions, scope, hoisting, and why understanding the call stack changes everything.
mods.body:
A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task. Functions are first-class citizens in JavaScript — they can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions.

Function Declarations

Named functions that are hoisted — you can call them before they appear in the code.

// Declaration
function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

console.log(greet("Sarah")); // "Hello, Sarah!"

// Hoisting in action — this WORKS
greet("Early bird");
function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}

Function Expressions

Functions assigned to variables. They are NOT hoisted — you must define them before calling.

const greet = function(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
};

// Anonymous function assigned to 'greet'
// Must be defined before use!

Arrow Functions (ES6)

Concise syntax. They have lexical this — they inherit this from the surrounding scope. This makes them perfect for callbacks.

// Traditional
const add = function(a, b) {
  return a + b;
};

// Arrow function
const add = (a, b) => {
  return a + b;
};

// Implicit return (no curly braces needed for single expressions)
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const square = x => x * x;        // single param needs no parens
const greet = () => "Hello!";     // no params need empty parens

// Perfect for array methods
const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]
Arrow functions have no this of their own. Do not use them as object methods if you need to reference the object with this.

Default Parameters

function createUser(name, role = "user", isActive = true) {
  return { name, role, isActive };
}

createUser("Alex");                    // { name: "Alex", role: "user", isActive: true }
createUser("Alex", "admin", false);    // { name: "Alex", role: "admin", isActive: false }

Rest Parameters (...args)

Collect remaining arguments into a real array.

function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}

sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10
sum(10, 20);     // 30

Scope: Where Variables Live

Scope determines where a variable is accessible.

const globalVar = "I am global";

function outer() {
  const outerVar = "I am in outer";

  function inner() {
    const innerVar = "I am in inner";
    console.log(globalVar);  // ✅ Accessible
    console.log(outerVar);   // ✅ Accessible (closure!)
    console.log(innerVar);   // ✅ Accessible
  }

  inner();
  // console.log(innerVar);  // ❌ ReferenceError!
}

outer();

The Call Stack

JavaScript uses a call stack to track function execution. When a function is called, it is pushed onto the stack. When it returns, it is popped off.

function first() {
  console.log("First");
  second();
}
function second() {
  console.log("Second");
  third();
}
function third() {
  console.log("Third");
}

first();
// Call Stack: first() → second() → third() → pop → pop → pop

mods.title: Arrays & Objects Mastery
mods.excerpt: Data is everything. Master arrays, objects, destructuring, spread syntax, and the powerful built-in methods that make JavaScript data manipulation a joy.
mods.body:
Arrays and objects are the two primary data structures in JavaScript. Arrays store ordered collections. Objects store keyed collections. Together, they power virtually every application.

Arrays: Ordered Collections

const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
const mixed = [42, "hello", true, { name: "Alex" }, [1, 2]];

// Access by index (0-based)
console.log(fruits[0]); // "apple"
console.log(fruits.length); // 3

// Add/remove
fruits.push("date");       // Add to end
fruits.pop();              // Remove from end
fruits.unshift("avocado"); // Add to start
fruits.shift();            // Remove from start

The Big Three: map, filter, reduce

These methods transform arrays declaratively — no manual loops needed.

const users = [
  { name: "Alice", age: 25, role: "admin" },
  { name: "Bob", age: 30, role: "user" },
  { name: "Carol", age: 22, role: "user" },
  { name: "David", age: 35, role: "editor" }
];

// map — transform every element
const names = users.map(u => u.name);
// ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "David"]

// filter — keep elements matching a condition
const adults = users.filter(u => u.age >= 25);
// [{Alice, 25}, {Bob, 30}, {David, 35}]

// reduce — accumulate to a single value
const totalAge = users.reduce((sum, u) => sum + u.age, 0);
// 112

// Chain them together!
const adminNames = users
  .filter(u => u.role === "admin")
  .map(u => u.name.toUpperCase());
// ["ALICE"]

Other Essential Array Methods

const nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9];

nums.find(n => n > 4);        // 5 (first match)
nums.findIndex(n => n > 4);   // 4 (index of first match)
nums.some(n => n > 8);        // true (at least one matches)
nums.every(n => n > 0);       // true (all match)
nums.includes(5);             // true
nums.indexOf(1);              // 1 (first occurrence)
nums.lastIndexOf(1);          // 3 (last occurrence)
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);   // [1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9]
nums.reverse();               // [9, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1]
nums.slice(1, 4);             // [5, 4, 3] (non-destructive)
nums.splice(2, 1);            // Removes 1 element at index 2

Objects: Keyed Collections

const user = {
  name: "Sarah",
  age: 28,
  isAdmin: false,
  "favorite color": "teal",  // quoted key with space
  greet() {
    return `Hi, I am ${this.name}`;
  }
};

// Access properties
console.log(user.name);              // dot notation
console.log(user["favorite color"]); // bracket notation (dynamic keys)

// Add/modify/delete
user.email = "sarah@example.com";
user.age = 29;
delete user.isAdmin;

// Check if property exists
console.log("name" in user);         // true
console.log(user.hasOwnProperty("age")); // true

Destructuring

Extract values from arrays and objects into distinct variables.

// Array destructuring
const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
// first = 10, second = 20, rest = [30, 40, 50]

// Skip elements
const [a, , c] = [1, 2, 3]; // a = 1, c = 3

// Object destructuring
const { name, age, role = "guest" } = user;
// Extracts name and age. If role does not exist, defaults to "guest"

// Rename while destructuring
const { name: fullName, age: yearsOld } = user;

// Nested destructuring
const company = {
  ceo: { name: "Elon", age: 52 },
  founded: 2003
};
const { ceo: { name: ceoName } } = company;
// ceoName = "Elon"

Spread Operator (...)

// Copy arrays (shallow)
const original = [1, 2, 3];
const copy = [...original];

// Merge arrays
const merged = [...[1, 2], ...[3, 4]]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]

// Copy objects (shallow)
const userCopy = { ...user, role: "admin" };
// Copies user, then overwrites role to "admin"

// Spread in function calls
const nums = [5, 1, 8];
Math.max(...nums); // 8 (same as Math.max(5, 1, 8))

Set — Unique Values

const ids = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3];
const uniqueIds = [...new Set(ids)]; // [1, 2, 3]

const tags = new Set();
tags.add("js");
tags.add("web");
tags.add("js"); // ignored — already exists
tags.has("js"); // true
tags.delete("web");
tags.size; // 1

mods.title: The DOM & Event Handling
mods.excerpt: Bridge the gap between static HTML and dynamic applications. Learn to select, create, modify elements, handle user events, and build interactive UIs from scratch.
mods.body:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree-like representation of your HTML document. JavaScript can read this tree, modify it, and respond to user interactions — turning static pages into living applications.

The DOM Tree

Every HTML element becomes a node in the DOM tree. The root is document, which contains <html>, which contains <head> and <body>, and so on.

<!-- HTML -->
<div id="app">
  <h1 class="title">Hello</h1>
  <button class="btn">Click me</button>
</div>

// JavaScript — the DOM representation:
document
  └── html
       └── body
            └── div#app
                 ├── h1.title ("Hello")
                 └── button.btn ("Click me")

Selecting Elements

// Modern, flexible selector (returns first match)
const title = document.querySelector('.title');
const app = document.querySelector('#app');

// Select all matching elements (returns NodeList)
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('.btn');
buttons.forEach(btn => console.log(btn.textContent));

// Older methods (still valid)
document.getElementById('app');           // single element by ID
document.getElementsByClassName('btn');   // HTMLCollection (live!)
document.getElementsByTagName('div');     // HTMLCollection (live!)
querySelectorAll vs getElementsByClassName: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList. getElementsBy* returns a live HTMLCollection that updates automatically when the DOM changes. Prefer querySelectorAll for predictability.

Modifying the DOM

const title = document.querySelector('.title');

// Change text (safe — treats as text, not HTML)
title.textContent = "Welcome to JS Mastery!";

// Change HTML (be careful — can execute scripts, XSS risk!)
title.innerHTML = "<em>Welcome</em> to JS Mastery!";

// Change styles (inline styles — use classes instead for maintainability)
title.style.color = "#c8f135";
title.style.fontSize = "2rem";
title.style.backgroundColor = "#0a0a0a";

// Better: toggle classes
title.classList.add('highlight');
title.classList.remove('highlight');
title.classList.toggle('active');   // add if absent, remove if present
title.classList.contains('active'); // true/false

// Attributes
title.setAttribute('data-id', '123');
console.log(title.getAttribute('data-id')); // "123"
title.removeAttribute('data-id');

Creating & Removing Elements

// Create element
const newCard = document.createElement('div');
newCard.className = 'card';
newCard.textContent = 'I am new!';

// Add to DOM
const container = document.querySelector('.container');
container.appendChild(newCard);        // add as last child
container.prepend(newCard);            // add as first child
container.insertBefore(newCard, container.firstChild);

// Modern: insertAdjacentElement
container.insertAdjacentElement('beforeend', newCard);
// Options: 'beforebegin', 'afterbegin', 'beforeend', 'afterend'

// Remove element
newCard.remove(); // Modern way
// container.removeChild(newCard); // Older way

Event Listeners

const btn = document.querySelector('.btn');

// Add listener
btn.addEventListener('click', function(event) {
  console.log('Button clicked!');
  console.log(event.target);        // the element that was clicked
  console.log(event.type);          // "click"
  console.log(event.clientX, event.clientY); // click coordinates
});

// Named function (easier to remove later)
function handleClick(e) {
  console.log('Clicked:', e.target.textContent);
}
btn.addEventListener('click', handleClick);
btn.removeEventListener('click', handleClick); // Clean up!

// Common events
// 'click', 'dblclick', 'mouseenter', 'mouseleave'
// 'keydown', 'keyup', 'keypress'
// 'submit', 'change', 'input', 'focus', 'blur'
// 'scroll', 'resize', 'load', 'DOMContentLoaded'

Event Delegation

Instead of adding listeners to every child, add ONE listener to the parent. Events bubble up from the target to ancestors.

// ❌ Bad: adding listener to every button
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('.todo-btn');
buttons.forEach(btn => btn.addEventListener('click', deleteTodo));

// ✅ Good: one listener on the parent
const todoList = document.querySelector('.todo-list');
todoList.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
  // Check if the clicked element (or its ancestor) matches
  if (e.target.closest('.delete-btn')) {
    const todoItem = e.target.closest('.todo-item');
    todoItem.remove();
  }
});

// This works even for buttons added AFTER the listener is set!

Event Bubbling vs Capturing

// Bubbling (default): child → parent → grandparent
// Capturing: grandparent → parent → child

// Use capturing by passing true as third argument
document.body.addEventListener('click', handler, true);

// Stop propagation
btn.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
  e.stopPropagation(); // Do not bubble up to parents
  e.preventDefault();  // Prevent default browser behavior (e.g., form submit)
});

mods.title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+)
mods.excerpt: Level up your syntax. Master let/const, template literals, enhanced object literals, default parameters, modules, and all the features that make modern JS beautiful.
mods.body:
ES6 (released in 2015) was a revolution for JavaScript. It introduced syntax that makes code cleaner, safer, and more expressive. Every modern codebase uses these features — mastering them is non-negotiable.

let & const: Block-Scoped Variables

Before ES6, var was the only option. It had function scope and was hoisted with an initial value of undefined — a recipe for bugs.

// var has function scope
function example() {
  if (true) {
    var x = 10;
  }
  console.log(x); // 10 — accessible outside the block!
}

// let has BLOCK scope
function example() {
  if (true) {
    let y = 10;
    const z = 20;
  }
  // console.log(y); // ❌ ReferenceError!
  // console.log(z); // ❌ ReferenceError!
}

// const prevents reassignment
const PI = 3.14159;
// PI = 3; // ❌ TypeError!

// But objects/arrays can still be mutated
const user = { name: "Alex" };
user.name = "Sam"; // ✅ Allowed

Template Literals

const name = "world";

// Multi-line strings
const poem = `
  Roses are red,
  Violets are blue,
  JavaScript is awesome,
  And so are you.
`;

// Expression interpolation
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}!`;

// Expression evaluation
const a = 5, b = 10;
console.log(`Fifteen is ${a + b}`); // "Fifteen is 15"

// Tagged templates (advanced)
function highlight(strings, ...values) {
  return strings.reduce((result, str, i) => {
    return result + str + (values[i] ? `${values[i]}` : '');
  }, '');
}
const name = "Alice", age = 30;
highlight`Name: ${name}, Age: ${age}`;
// "Name: Alice, Age: 30"

Enhanced Object Literals

const name = "Sarah";
const age = 28;

// ES5
const user = {
  name: name,
  age: age,
  greet: function() {
    return "Hello";
  }
};

// ES6 — shorthand properties & methods
const user = {
  name,        // same as name: name
  age,         // same as age: age
  greet() {    // shorthand method
    return `Hello, I am ${this.name}`;
  },
  ['user_' + id]: true  // computed property names
};

Modules: import / export

Modules let you split code into reusable files. Each module has its own scope.

// math.js — exporting
export const PI = 3.14159;

export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

export default function multiply(a, b) {
  return a * b;
}

// main.js — importing
import multiply, { add, PI } from './math.js';
import * as math from './math.js';  // namespace import

console.log(add(2, 3));        // 5
console.log(multiply(2, 3));   // 6
console.log(math.PI);          // 3.14159

Optional Chaining (ES2020)

Safely access nested properties without checking each level.

const user = {
  profile: {
    // name is missing!
  }
};

// ❌ Old way
const name = user && user.profile && user.profile.name;

// ✅ Optional chaining
const name = user?.profile?.name; // undefined (no error!)

// With nullish coalescing (??)
const displayName = user?.profile?.name ?? "Anonymous";
// ?? only falls back on null or undefined (not 0, "", or false)

Nullish Coalescing (??)

const count = 0;
const value1 = count || 10;  // 10 (0 is falsy!)
const value2 = count ?? 10;  // 0 (0 is not null/undefined!)

const name = null;
const display = name ?? "Guest"; // "Guest"

mods.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
mods.excerpt: The browser cannot freeze while waiting for data. Master the Event Loop, Promises, async/await, Fetch API, and understand how JavaScript handles concurrency under the hood.

mods.title: Advanced Functions & Closures
mods.excerpt: Unlock the true power of JavaScript functions. Master closures, higher-order functions, currying, memoization, and generators — the tools that senior developers use daily.

mods.title: OOP in JavaScript
mods.excerpt: JavaScript is not class-based — it is prototype-based. Understand prototypes, the this keyword, classes (syntactic sugar), inheritance, and composition over inheritance.

mods.title: Error Handling & Debugging
mods.excerpt: Bugs are inevitable. Learn to catch them gracefully with try/catch/finally, create custom errors, use the debugger, and master console methods that most developers never touch.

mods.title: Modules, Bundlers & Tooling
mods.excerpt: Production code is not just files — it is an ecosystem. Learn ES modules, npm, Webpack, Vite, Babel, and the build pipeline that transforms your code for the real world.

mods.title: Testing & Performance
mods.excerpt: A great site is fast and reliable. Learn unit testing with Jest, performance optimization, memory management, and how to write code that scales under real-world load.
